name: workbench
description:
The frame a desktop app lives in: a fixed rail, a scrolling main region, and nothing that scrolls the whole window.

Named `workbench` and not `app-shell` for a reason worth recording. `app-shell` is already a legacy class — six surfaces use it to mean 'the page wrapper', a min-height and a ground — and defining a unit under the same name silently restyled every one of them into a two-column grid. Nothing reported it: the class resolved, the CSS was valid, and the docs page simply rendered with its content pushed 700px to the right. A new unit taking a name the old vocabulary still owns is the one migration hazard that has no gate.

What the unit gets right is `min-block-size: 0` on the scrolling child. A grid child defaults to `min-height: auto` and refuses to shrink below its content, so a main region full of a long list does not scroll — it grows, the page scrolls instead, and the rail scrolls away with it. Every app that has ever had 'the sidebar disappears when I scroll' has had this bug.

base.$description:
`100dvh`, not `100vh` — on a phone `vh` is the viewport WITHOUT the browser chrome, so a full-height shell is taller than the screen and the bottom of it sits under the address bar until you scroll.

CONTAINER. This unit establishes an inline-size container named after itself, so anything inside it can respond to the width of THIS BOX rather than to the width of the window. That is the difference that matters for a design system: a composite dropped into a 320px sidebar and the same composite on a 320px phone are the same situation, and a viewport query calls them different ones. The library carries no viewport media query anywhere for exactly this reason — the only `@media` in it is `prefers-reduced-motion`, which is a person's setting and not a size.

`inline-size: 100%` is the container's REQUIRED companion, not a preference. `container-type: inline-size` makes the box's width independent of its contents — that is the containment being asked for — so a container with no width of its own has nothing left to size from and collapses to zero. This unit did: centred in a grid it became a column of single words. A container fills what it is given and bounds itself with `max-inline-size`; it never sizes to its text.

THE ONE PLACE `dvh` IS ALLOWED. This unit is the application root — the box the viewport actually is — so measuring the viewport here is the unit measuring itself. Everywhere else in the library a viewport unit means a component reading a box it does not own, which is what makes a hero in a preview card ask for 85% of the monitor. `100dvh` and not `100vh`: on a phone `vh` excludes the browser chrome, so a full-height shell is taller than the screen and its bottom sits under the address bar until you scroll.

THE SHELL DECLARES THE TRACK. `var(--workbench-rail, 16rem)`, not `auto`. `auto` is the layout declining to decide, which hands the decision back to the content — and a rail whose content is a container then has nothing to size from and collapses to zero. That is what emptied the docs page's navigation.

The rule the whole library follows: the LAYOUT sizes the slot, the unit fills it. A composite that picks its own width is arguing with the thing that positioned it.

rail.$description: Where the `sidebar` goes, and nothing else. Fixed width, its own scroll — it does not scroll with the main region, which is the entire point of the shell. It used to carry a `marker` part of its own: a shell that holds no items had a declaration for marking the current one, while `sidebar` described a marker in prose and drew none. The marker now lives with the items it marks, and this part only positions the rail.

main.$description: `min-inline-size: 0` AND `min-block-size: 0`. Both are load-bearing and neither is obvious: a grid child defaults to `auto` on both axes, so without them a wide table widens the column and a long list refuses to shrink — and the shell scrolls instead of the region inside it.

aside.$description: An optional third column — an inspector, a detail pane. Hidden below the breakpoint rather than stacked, because a detail pane under a list on a phone is a second page pretending to be a column.

panes.$description: How many columns the shell has. Declared rather than inferred, so the grid does not have to guess from what is slotted.

icons.$description: An icon-only rail. Every item still needs a label — a rail of unlabelled glyphs is a navigation nobody can read. It changes the TRACK, not the child's width: the shell owns the column.

wide.$description: A wider rail, for an index with long labels or counts.

a11y.note: One `<main>`, once per page — it is the skip-link target and the landmark a screen-reader user jumps to. The rail is a `<nav>` with a label. On an icon-only rail every item keeps a visible-to-assistive-tech label: an icon with a tooltip is not a label, because a tooltip needs hover. WCAG 2.4.11: the rail is fixed, so anything focusable in main must not be able to scroll underneath it.
